extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of Popular Science Monthly — naturalists, scientists, artists, and informed lay readers interested in science and art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and judging magazine essays, reviews, and correspondence about art and popular science (including natural-history notes, observational reports, and book reviews). Emphasizes qualities that make artistic work original and scientific writing rigorous and accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful delineation and fitness to modern taste
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing sixteenth- and nineteenth-century pictures, the charm of modern work is in the truthful delineation of scenery and character, and in a certain reflection of our experiences and fitness as related to the drift of our imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer nature mirrored by modern masters; modern works show 'reality and daylight effect' suited to the modern eye and taste. Ancient methods or allegorical subjects, however impressive in coloring (e.g., Rubens, Murillo), are often not suited to present standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to propriety and probability in design
rubrics_metrics.description: A highly developed sense of humor and taste in art requires close attention to propriety and probability in every design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical scientific criticism can expose ludicrous disregard for physical laws in art (example: angels drawn without regard to equilibrium). Artists should ensure designs are plausible within observed reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from schools (avoid slavish 'school' membership)
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'school of art' is objectionable when it means more than a preparatory course; an artist ought to be independent of all schools, or have a touch of all in his work, otherwise his liberty will be restricted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use schools only for rudimentary training; develop individual vision rather than adopt special colors or tones advocated by conformists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality sustained by truth to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality generally shows strongest advantage; the unprecedented qualities in a work of genius are always sustained by a certain truth to nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitators fail because they 'see the effect after it has been rendered' and cannot perceive similar effects in nature; thus originality must be rooted in truthful observation rather than trickery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing originality with mannerism
rubrics_metrics.description: Conservative critics often misapply 'mannerism' to novel work; mannerism properly means tasteless uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not abandon a forcible system of treatment simply because critics call it mannerism; the danger of powerful methods becoming tedious repetitions is slight if the artist maintains continuous growth and transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous growth and transformative practice
rubrics_metrics.description: True merit shows continuous growth: individuality accompanied by constant transformations, absorbing new material and finding new methods of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should develop by close attention to natural tendencies, persist through failures, and labor conscientiously to evolve originality into lasting work and higher adaptation to nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek natural effects locally, not just foreign models
rubrics_metrics.description: After suitable instruction, the artist must look for natural effects in the world directly around him, and not in Rome or in Paris.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delineate impressions as seen locally; do not be discouraged by failures—close attention to one's own tendencies will reveal true points of strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply exact investigation to scientific hypotheses (avoid over-speculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In biological and natural-science work, enough has been done in philosophizing; the task now is to apply the test of exact investigation to hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers (e.g., Darwinists, Haeckel's school) should concentrate on observation and experiment and pursue rigorous investigation of facts rather than fanciful hypothetical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on variability: measure extent and conditions experimentally
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the problems raised by evolution, variability in organisms is fundamental; we must determine to what extent and under what conditions variability is manifested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variability should be traced by exact investigation to its limits and efficient causes; harmonize conflicting opinions by closer experimental research and careful observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear definition of scope, point of view, and organized treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific works should define the 'external conditions of existence' accurately, state the point of view, and present a clear plan of discussion (as Semper's division into two parts and twelve chapters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize material into logically titled chapters (e.g., influence of food, light, temperature, water, etc.); append notes and a copious alphabetical index; include maps and illustrations where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance popular exposition with scientific accuracy for general readers
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing a general audience (e.g., Lowell lectures turned into book), present material as popular as the nature of the subject permits while maintaining scientific correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear exposition that is accessible yet not speculative; include aids (maps, woodcuts) and careful examples; avoid overstating or simplifying to the point of misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of good popular natural-history books for youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Books aimed at young readers should have a marvelously simple yet scientific style, give food for thought and future study, and convey a philosophical glow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within practical length and illustration limits, avoid misleading terminology (criticizes use of 'slime' for protoplasm; suggests 'jelly' as more appropriate); expect fewer technical details but ensure accuracy and inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and explicitness in mathematical/technical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical works should begin with precise definitions, discuss symbols and notation (including necessary enlargements/modifications), and state which algebraic principles are adopted or rejected (e.g., distributive and associative accepted; commutative not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit scope where necessary (Peirce limits to algebras handling ≤6 distinct qualities); define linear algebras (expressions reducible to algebraic sums of terms each expressive of a single quality); provide discussion and commentary—lack of commentary forces patient self-examination by readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide representative examples but also commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Listing many possible cases (e.g., nearly a hundred algebras) is useful, but the reader benefits from commentary explaining significance and prior occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without explanatory commentary, readers may have to laboriously discover which cases matter; explicit notes on noteworthy examples (e.g., only three known previously) help orient the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for observational natural-history correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Good natural-history letters/reporting include origin of specimens, habitat description, behavioral details, changes over time, and practical consequences (e.g., spread in new environment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include hypothesized causes for observed phenomena (example: ink color change attributed to formic acid discharged by ants), note preventive measures tried (e.g., daily chalk line as barrier), and indicate whether phenomena damage or merely affect objects (ants attracted to fresh ink but not damaging paper).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for astronomical/field observation reports
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful observational report records direction, elevation above horizon, rate of motion, duration of visibility, description of trails or luminous phenomena, times of observation, and local reaction if noteworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide exact times (e.g., 'visible from 5.27 until 5.45 o'clock'), describe peculiar behavior of the phenomenon (long-lived luminous 'tail', zigzagging streak), and note whether the observation is unusual in the locality.
